slice_results.behavior_summary: When called, the code accesses user-selected image files via browser File APIs, reads and converts them to base64 data URLs, processes images to generate thumbnails or full photos, and stores them in an internal static library map. It uses sensitive file operations (FileReader, Blob creation) and DOM manipulation to handle file input elements and image processing. No network or system execution occurs, and no suspicious hardcoded IPs, URLs, or commands are present, resulting in local image library management without external data exfiltration or code execution.
slice_results.explanation: [LLM Judgment: Benign] The analyzed code is a browser-based photo library proxy that manages user-selected image files locally. It uses standard browser File APIs (FileReader, Blob, Image) and DOM manipulation to allow users to select image files, process them into thumbnails or full photos, and store them in an internal map. There is no network communication, no external data exfiltration, no system command execution, and no obfuscation. The code explicitly requires user interaction to select files and does not access any camera or screen capture APIs automatically. Compared to the known malicious patterns, which involve automated webcam or screenshot capture and network exfiltration, this code lacks any such behavior. The use of sensitive APIs here is legitimate and expected for local image processing in a browser environment.

slice_results.explanation: [LLM Judgment: Benign] The analyzed code is a Cordova plugin module designed to interact with the device's photo library. It uses standard Cordova exec calls to request authorization, retrieve photos and thumbnails, save images and videos, and manage caching. There is no evidence of network communication, data exfiltration, shell command execution, or obfuscation. The code constructs custom URL schemes for local photo access and converts data to Blob objects for local use. Compared to the known malicious patterns, which involve webcam activation, screenshot capture, credential stealing via child processes, and network exfiltration to hardcoded external servers, this code does not exhibit any similar suspicious behavior or API usage. The presence of photo library access is expected for a photo management plugin and does not imply malicious intent. Therefore, the code is considered benign with very low confidence of maliciousness.

malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: A legitimate file-sharing client or backup tool may upload files, but only with user consent and clear intent.
key_indicators: Hardcoded upload endpoint (telegra.ph)
No user notification or consent before upload
Automated network exfiltration of file data

package_info.why_malicious: The package contains obfuscated JavaScript code that, at runtime, exfiltrates user files to multiple hardcoded external file-sharing services without user consent. It automates unauthorized data uploads to suspicious endpoints, using randomized filenames and evasion techniques, making it a tool for covert data exfiltration and a clear indicator of compromise.

attack_chain.action: Prepare file data for upload by creating form-data with randomized filenames.
attack_chain.leads_to: File data is ready for exfiltration.

attack_chain.action: Upload file data to external file-sharing services via HTTP POST requests, targeting multiple hardcoded endpoints.
attack_chain.leads_to: Files are exfiltrated to attacker-controlled endpoints.

attack_chain.action: Monitor the package file for changes and reload dynamically to evade detection or enable code updates.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code persists and can be updated without user awareness.

behavioral_signatures: Automated creation of form-data from arbitrary file buffers at runtime
Silent HTTP POST requests to known file-sharing endpoints without user interaction
Use of fake or randomized User-Agent headers in network requests to evade detection
Self-watching and hot-reloading of package files at runtime using fs.watchFile
file_indicators: Obfuscated JavaScript in main package file
References to file-sharing endpoints such as telegra.ph, uguu.se, catbox.moe, pomf2.lain.la, uploadcare.com, tmpfiles.org, itzpire.site, skizo.tech
fs.watchFile usage targeting __filename in JavaScript files
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor JavaScript packages for creation of form-data from arbitrary file buffers and automated HTTP POST requests to known file-sharing endpoints, especially if these actions occur without user interaction. Flag any use of fs.watchFile on the package's own file (__filename), and inspect for obfuscated code or hardcoded references to suspicious upload URLs. Network monitoring should alert on outbound POST requests to the listed file-sharing domains. Correlate these behaviors to identify covert data exfiltration attempts.

slice_results.behavior_summary: When called, the code executes cordova.exec to access photo library data and metadata, including albums, authorization status, thumbnails, and photos. It constructs custom URLs with the cdvphotolibrary:// scheme for accessing photos and thumbnails, encodes parameters safely, and processes binary photo data into Blob objects. No external network or file system operations occur; the code interacts with device APIs to read and expose photo library content, enabling photo access and manipulation within the app.
slice_results.explanation: [LLM Judgment: Benign] The analyzed code is a Cordova plugin interface for accessing and manipulating the device's photo library. It uses the standard Cordova exec API to request photo library data, thumbnails, and photos, and constructs custom URLs with a specific scheme (cdvphotolibrary://) for internal referencing. There is no evidence of network exfiltration, remote command execution, or covert camera activation. The code does not access the webcam or screen, nor does it send data to external servers. It only interacts with device APIs to read and expose photo library content with user-initiated callbacks. Compared to the known malicious patterns, which involve unauthorized webcam activation, screenshot capture, or remote command-based photo capture and exfiltration, this code lacks any such suspicious or malicious behavior. The presence of photo library access is expected in legitimate apps that manage photos. No obfuscation or suspicious system manipulation is present.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, the code activates the user's webcam using node-webcam, captures an image, and exfiltrates the photo data to a remote server, resulting in a privacy violation.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Accessing the webcam and sending images externally without user consent is a hallmark of spyware and a severe privacy violation.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate npm packages should not access the webcam or exfiltrate images without explicit user consent and notification.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Video conferencing or camera applications may access the webcam, but only with user permission and clear indication.
key_indicators: Use of node-webcam or similar webcam access modules
Automated webcam activation and image capture
Network exfiltration of webcam images or video data

execution_context.file_location: main application file or a helper module

package_info.why_malicious: The package is malicious because it abuses ChromePass, a legitimate password-recovery tool for Google Chrome, to steal user credentials. It also provides advanced surveillance and system compromise capabilities, including unauthorized access to the user's screen, webcam, filesystem, and shell, with automated exfiltration of sensitive data to remote servers. These behaviors are highly indicative of malware and pose significant privacy and security risks.

attack_chain.action: User installs or runs the malicious npm package.
Malware executes ChromePass to extract Chrome passwords and exfiltrates them.
Malware captures screenshots and exfiltrates them.
Malware activates webcam, captures images, and exfiltrates them.
Malware lists user directories and exfiltrates directory listings.
Malware executes arbitrary shell commands and exfiltrates the results.
attack_chain.leads_to: Full system compromise and persistent access.

behavioral_signatures: Execution of ChromePass.exe or other credential extraction tools from within npm package code
Unusual access to webcam or screen capture APIs (e.g., node-webcam, screenshot-desktop) without user interaction
Automated directory listing of user or system folders followed by network exfiltration
Remote shell command execution via child_process.exec or similar APIs with exfiltration of outputs
file_indicators: Presence of ChromePass.exe bundled or downloaded in the package directory
Creation of temporary files such as passwords.txt or screenshot images in user directories
Unexpected image files (e.g., test_picture.jpg) or directory listings in temporary or user folders
network_indicators: Outbound connections to unknown or suspicious remote servers immediately after credential, image, or directory data is generated
Exfiltration of credential files (e.g., passwords.txt), screenshots, webcam images, or command outputs via HTTP, HTTPS, or other protocols
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor npm packages for execution of external tools like ChromePass.exe, access to webcam or screen capture APIs (e.g., node-webcam, screenshot-desktop), and unexpected network activity following sensitive data access. Flag packages that attempt to exfiltrate files, images, or command outputs. Scan for bundled binaries such as ChromePass.exe and temporary files like passwords.txt or screenshot images in user directories. Use endpoint protection to detect suspicious child_process executions, automated directory listings, and network exfiltration attempts. Correlate behavioral, file, and network indicators to identify malicious activity.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, the code captures screenshots and webcam images using system APIs or npm modules, then exfiltrates the captured media to a remote server via network requests, resulting in unauthorized surveillance.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Accessing the screen and camera without user consent and sending the data externally is a hallmark of spyware and privacy violation.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal npm packages should not access or exfiltrate screen or camera data unless explicitly designed for such purposes with user awareness and consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Video conferencing or screenshot tools may access these resources, but only with user consent and without silent exfiltration to unknown servers.
key_indicators: Use of screenshot-desktop or node-webcam modules for image capture
Silent capture of screenshots or webcam images without user notification
Network exfiltration of image data to remote servers
Absence of user prompts or consent dialogs for camera/screen access

execution_context.file_location: main JavaScript file or auxiliary modules

package_info.why_malicious: The package is considered malicious because it abuses a legitimate password-recovery tool (ChromePass) to steal credentials from Google Chrome, and provides additional capabilities such as unauthorized screen and camera access, directory enumeration, and remote shell command execution. These behaviors are not expected in legitimate npm packages and indicate clear intent to exfiltrate sensitive user data and enable remote control of the victim's system.

attack_chain.action: Malicious npm package is installed on the victim's system.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of malicious code at runtime

attack_chain.action: At runtime, the package executes ChromePass.exe to extract Chrome passwords and exfiltrates them to a remote server.
The package captures screenshots and webcam images, then exfiltrates them to a remote server.
The package lists directories on the victim's filesystem and sends the information to a remote server.
The package enables remote shell command execution, allowing attackers to control the victim's system and maintain persistence.

behavioral_signatures: Execution of ChromePass.exe or similar credential extraction tools from within npm packages
Silent screenshot or webcam capture using screenshot-desktop or node-webcam modules followed by network exfiltration
Automated directory listing of user or system directories and exfiltration of file lists
Remote command execution via child_process.exec or similar APIs, especially when commands originate from network sources
file_indicators: Bundled or downloaded ChromePass.exe binary within the package directory
Creation of temporary files such as passwords.txt in user-accessible directories
Unusual or unauthorized use of screenshot-desktop or node-webcam modules in non-UI npm packages
network_indicators: Outbound connections to known command-and-control or exfiltration domains immediately after package installation or execution
HTTP POST requests containing credential dumps, screenshots, webcam images, or directory listings
Unusual network traffic patterns from node.js processes, especially following execution of external binaries or system commands
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for npm packages that execute external binaries such as ChromePass.exe, access camera or screen APIs, or perform directory listing and exfiltration. Flag packages that initiate outbound network connections immediately after installation or at runtime, especially those sending sensitive files, images, or command outputs. Use endpoint security tools to detect suspicious process execution and network activity originating from node.js processes, and correlate with the presence of bundled binaries or unauthorized use of system resources.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, upon receiving a remote command from the C2 server, the code activates the device camera, captures a photo, and transmits the image data to the attacker, enabling covert surveillance without user awareness.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Remotely triggering the camera to take photos and exfiltrate images without user interaction is a severe privacy violation and a common tactic in RATs for surveillance.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal Android apps require explicit user action and visible UI to access the camera, and do not transmit captured images to unknown servers without user consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Video conferencing or camera apps use the camera, but only with user consent, visible UI, and clear data handling policies.
key_indicators: Remote command-based camera activation
Silent photo capture and exfiltration
No user notification or visible UI during camera use
Transmission of image data to external C2 server

execution_context.file_location: Android service or broadcast receiver (e.g., CommandReceiver.java)

package_info.package_versions: All versions (open-source, actively used in campaigns)
package_info.why_malicious: Rafel RAT is a remote administration tool for Android that enables full device compromise, including unauthorized data exfiltration, covert surveillance, remote command execution, and ransomware deployment. It is actively leveraged in espionage and cybercrime campaigns, providing attackers with persistent, unauthorized access and control over victim devices.

attack_chain.action: Victim installs the trojanized Android app (Rafel RAT) on their device.
attack_chain.leads_to: Initial execution and background service start

attack_chain.action: On first run, the malware collects device info and contacts, then exfiltrates them to the C2 server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains intelligence on the victim

attack_chain.action: The malware maintains persistence and awaits commands from the C2 server.
Upon receiving commands, the malware can activate the camera for surveillance, send SMS, or encrypt files.

behavioral_signatures: Android app requesting excessive permissions (contacts, SMS, camera, microphone, location, etc.)
Background exfiltration of contacts, device info, or media files to external servers
Remote command-and-control communication over HTTP(S) with external infrastructure
Silent activation of camera or microphone without user interaction
Unsolicited SMS sending from the device without user action
On-device file encryption triggered remotely by C2 commands
file_indicators: APK files with suspicious or generic names unrelated to legitimate apps
Presence of hardcoded C2 URLs or IP addresses in app resources or code
Unusual use of Android services or broadcast receivers for remote command execution
network_indicators: Outbound connections to known Rafel RAT C2 domains or IP addresses
Frequent HTTP(S) POST requests containing device data, contacts, or media files
Unusual traffic patterns from Android devices to untrusted or unrecognized servers
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor Android apps for excessive and unnecessary permission requests, especially those involving contacts, SMS, camera, microphone, and location. Analyze background network activity for exfiltration of sensitive data such as contacts, device info, or media files. Detect remote command execution by monitoring for silent camera or microphone activation, unsolicited SMS sending, or file encryption events. Use network monitoring to identify connections to known Rafel RAT C2 infrastructure and inspect outbound traffic for sensitive data leaks. Correlate behavioral, file, and network indicators to identify and block malicious activity.

matched_knowledge.source_package: Malicious Weather App (PoC exploiting CVE-2019-2234) (Android APK (Google Play/side-loaded))

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, upon receiving a C&C command, the code sends a crafted intent to the camera app to take a photo, stores the resulting image in accessible storage, and uploads the image file to a remote C&C server, enabling covert photo capture and exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The app programmatically triggers the camera to take photos without user interaction or holding the camera permission, exploiting a vulnerability to bypass Android's security model.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal apps require explicit user consent and the CAMERA permission to access the camera; this app bypasses those controls and initiates photo capture from the background.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate camera or automation apps may use camera intents, but only with user consent, visible UI, and proper permissions.
key_indicators: Background app sending camera capture intent without CAMERA permission
No user interaction required for photo capture
Captured images automatically uploaded to remote server

execution_context.file_location: malicious app main activity / background service

package_info.package_versions: All versions prior to patched Google Camera/Samsung Camera apps (pre-July 2019)
package_info.why_malicious: The package exploits a vulnerability in Android camera app intent handling (CVE-2019-2234) to bypass camera and microphone permissions, enabling covert photo, video, and audio capture, as well as exfiltration of sensitive data (including GPS metadata) to a remote C&C server. It maintains persistent C&C communication for remote exploitation, operating without user consent or awareness.

attack_chain.action: Malicious app is installed and establishes a persistent connection to the attacker's C&C server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Remote attacker can issue commands to the device.

attack_chain.action: Attacker issues command to take a photo, record video, or record audio (including during calls), triggering covert media capture.
attack_chain.leads_to: Device captures sensitive media (photos, videos, audio) without user knowledge.

attack_chain.action: Captured photos and videos are stored in accessible storage; app parses EXIF data for GPS location.
attack_chain.leads_to: Sensitive media and location data are prepared for exfiltration.

attack_chain.action: App uploads captured media and extracted GPS/location data to the attacker's C&C server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains access to private photos, videos, audio, and location data from the device.

behavioral_signatures: Background apps sending camera or video capture intents without holding CAMERA or MICROPHONE permissions
Apps accessing and parsing EXIF GPS metadata from photos or videos without user interaction
Persistent outbound connections to unknown servers from apps not expected to require continuous network access
Media capture events triggered by proximity sensor activity in background services
file_indicators: Unexpected photos or videos appearing in device camera roll or media storage
App accessing camera or media storage without user-initiated action or visible UI
Frequent or automated access to EXIF data in app logs or storage access patterns
network_indicators: Outbound connections to C&C infrastructure (unknown IPs/domains) from non-network-centric apps
Uploads of media files (photos, videos, audio) to remote servers without user action
Persistent TCP connections initiated by background services with no user-facing justification
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for apps that trigger camera or video capture intents without holding CAMERA or MICROPHONE permissions, especially if they only request storage permission. Flag apps that access EXIF GPS metadata or upload media files to external servers without user interaction. Use network monitoring to detect persistent outbound connections from apps not expected to maintain such connections. Alert on media capture events triggered by background services or proximity sensor events, and correlate with lack of user interaction or visible UI.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: During postinstall, the code reads image files (logo1.jpg, logo2.jpg, logo3.jpg), extracts ASCII payloads from their byte data, and if a threshold is met, dynamically executes the extracted string as JavaScript code, resulting in arbitrary code execution sourced from image-embedded payloads.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Extracting and executing code from image files is a classic steganography-based evasion technique, designed to bypass static analysis and conceal malicious payloads within seemingly benign files.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages do not extract and execute code from image files during installation, nor do they use dynamic code execution on data sourced from non-code files.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate image processing libraries may read and analyze image files, but never execute dynamically extracted code from image data.
key_indicators: Steganographic payload extraction from image files
Dynamic code execution using new Function() on extracted strings
Threshold-based trigger for code execution (payload length > 2000)
References to analyzepixels, convertertree, and imagebyte variables

package_info.why_malicious: The package is a trojanized clone of a legitimate library, containing concealed code that, during installation, extracts and executes a command-and-control (C2) payload hidden within image files. This enables remote code execution and exfiltration of command results, granting attackers persistent remote access to infected systems.

attack_chain.action: During installation, index.js spawns a detached process to execute dist/loadformat.js.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of the malicious loader script in a separate process.

attack_chain.action: dist/loadformat.js reads image files (logo1.jpg, logo2.jpg, logo3.jpg), extracts ASCII payloads, and dynamically executes code if a threshold is met.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of the C2 payload if present in the image files.

attack_chain.action: Extracted C2 payload registers the client with the attacker's server, polls for commands, executes them, and exfiltrates results.
attack_chain.leads_to: Full remote control of the infected system and exfiltration of command output.

behavioral_signatures: Postinstall script spawns detached Node.js processes using spawn/unref
Image files (logo1.jpg, logo2.jpg, logo3.jpg) are read and parsed for ASCII payloads during installation
Dynamic code execution via new Function() on data extracted from image files
Outbound HTTPS connections to hardcoded IP address 85.208.108.29 for registration, polling, and result exfiltration
Periodic polling for remote commands and execution of arbitrary shell commands
file_indicators: dist/loadformat.js
index.js containing spawn/unref logic targeting dist/loadformat.js
logo1.jpg, logo2.jpg, logo3.jpg in package root directory
References to analyzepixels, convertertree, and imagebyte variables in code
network_indicators: Outbound POST requests to /register and /post-result endpoints
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for npm packages that, during installation, spawn detached Node.js processes, read and parse image files for ASCII payloads, or dynamically execute code extracted from non-code files. Flag packages making outbound connections to hardcoded or suspicious IPs (e.g., 85.208.108.29) or exhibiting periodic polling for remote commands. Scan package contents for the presence of suspicious image files (logo1.jpg, logo2.jpg, logo3.jpg) and loader scripts (dist/loadformat.js), and inspect for code patterns involving analyzepixels, convertertree, and imagebyte.
